title: The Essentials of Breath-Based Buddha-Recitation
author: Zhanran
excerpt: [Ten thoughts in unbroken succession; repeated practice becomes second nature] This is a reliable guarantee of rebirth in the Pure Land. See the article "The Conditions for Rebirth in the Pure Land." [Unbroken succession] The thoughts of Buddha-recitation connect one to the next, uninterrupted by deluded thoughts. [Repeated practice becomes second nature] Through repeated practice it becomes instinct.

inline.s: Ten thoughts in unbroken succession; repeated practice becomes second nature.
[Ten thoughts in unbroken succession; repeated practice becomes second nature] This is a reliable guarantee of rebirth in the Pure Land. For details, see
The Conditions for Rebirth in the Pure Land

. [Unbroken succession] The thoughts of Buddha-recitation connect one to the next, uninterrupted by deluded thoughts. [Repeated practice becomes second nature] Through repeated practice it becomes instinct.

Breath-based Buddha-recitation is a wondrous method that both gathers in the mind and is easy to sustain, and it cultivates body and mind together. The method is this: breathing in and out through the nose
with abdominal breathing, reciting the Buddha's name along with the in-breath and the out-breath — on the in-breath silently reciting "A-mi" in the mind, on the out-breath silently reciting "Tuo-fo."
Of course, one may also recite "Amitābha Buddha" once on the in-breath and once on the out-breath.

This is the Precious King's method of following the breath. It lets breath-based recitation continue thought after thought until habit becomes nature: ten recitations, ten rebirths; a hundred recitations, a hundred rebirths.

[Cultivating body and mind together] A complete cultivation of body and mind. Cultivating the body means health, longevity, and happiness; cultivating the mind means awakening to the Way, realizing the Way, and putting an end to birth and death.
Master Feixi of the Tang dynasty says in his Precious King Treatise on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation:

"People in the world mostly use precious stones, crystal, diamond, bodhi seeds, or wooden beads as their recitation beads. I, however, use the out-breath and in-breath as my recitation beads. Calling the Buddha's name and following it with the breath, I have a great reliance
(pronounced shì hù)
, so why fear that when one breath does not return
one belongs to the next life! In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down I always use these beads; even when dull and drowsy, I fall asleep holding the Buddha in my mouth,
and as soon as I wake I continue.

Thus I am sure to see that Buddha in my dreams. As smoke rising from drilling a fire-stick is the precursor of flame, so when the dreaming does not cease, the samādhi is accomplished. To behold his jade-white urna face to face and personally receive his prediction of enlightenment — that is to be without the slightest failure."

Translation: People in the world mostly use precious stones, crystal, diamond, bodhi seeds, or wooden beads as their recitation beads. I use the out-breath and in-breath as my recitation beads. Calling the Buddha's name and following it with the breath, one has a great reliance: why fear that when a breath fails to return one belongs to the next life? In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down I always use these beads; even when dull and drowsy, I fall asleep holding the Buddha in my mouth, and the moment I wake I continue at once. Practicing in this way, one is sure to see Amitābha Buddha in dreams. As smoke rising from drilling a fire-stick is the precursor of flame, so if one sees the Buddha in dreams without cease, the samādhi of Buddha-recitation will be accomplished. To behold with one's own eyes the jade-white urna between Amitābha Buddha's brows and personally receive from him the prediction of rebirth — that is to be utterly without failure.

[Having a great reliance — why fear that when one breath does not return one belongs to the next life] Once breath-based Buddha-recitation has become second nature through long habituation, the final breath of one's life will certainly be a recitation of the Buddha's name, with no second thought; then of course one is reborn with right mindfulness at the end of life — why fear that a breath will not return? So breath-based recitation is a great reliance. [As smoke rises from drilling a fire-stick, the precursor of flame] When fire is drilled out of wood and smoke comes forth, it shows that flame will soon arise. Rising smoke is the sign that fire is about to start. Here it illustrates that seeing the Buddha in dreams is the sign that the samādhi of Buddha-recitation is being accomplished. [Drilling a fire-stick (suì)] Also written as "drilling a sui" with a variant character. Drilling a fire-stick to obtain fire is a primitive way of making fire; the sui is the tool used to obtain fire.
Master Yinguang greatly esteemed and praised breath-based Buddha-recitation. In a letter to Master Dixian he wrote:
"I
(the Master's self-reference)
have believed in the one Dharma of the Pure Land since leaving home life. But because
but
because)

of the obstruction of karmic hindrances, for twenty years I have idly frittered away the time. Though I recite the Buddha's name with my mouth, my mind takes no delight in the Way. Recently, urged on by your instruction, I vowed not to fail your grandmotherly kindness. Yet torpor and scatteredness
(torpor and distraction)

attack me in turn, and I remain as I was before. So each day I read more than ten pages of Pure Land scriptures to rouse a mind of surpassing diligence. When I came to the Precious King's method of following the breath
(that is, the instruction of Master Feixi above)
, I tried this method, and at once felt that deluded thoughts were no longer like the surging tide and tossing waves of before.
I think that in the course of time there will surely come a moment when the mist scatters and the clouds dissolve, and the sky and sun are fully seen.

......I also say that this one method alone fully encompasses the five contemplations that still the mind. If one can recite the Buddha's name following the breath, one encompasses the two contemplations of counting the breath and reciting the Buddha's name
(that is, it encompasses the contemplation of counting the breath, which stills distraction, and the contemplation of Buddha-recitation, which stills karmic hindrances)
. Moreover, when one gathers in the mind and recites the Buddha's name, the defiled mind can gradually be cut off
(stilling greed)
, anger and hatred will surely not blaze up
(stilling anger)
, and once torpor and distraction are gone, wisdom appears and delusion can be broken
(stilling delusion)
. This is again the method by which Mahāsthāmaprāpta gathers in all six sense faculties
(this is again the method of Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta: 'gather in all six sense faculties, and let pure mindfulness continue without interruption')

. I foolishly think that those who nowadays recite the Buddha's name in a careless, hurried way should probably not be told to rely on this method, lest, since they keep no count, they fall into laziness. But those who have a determined mind, if they do not rely on this method, will certainly find it hard to attain samādhi. You, Master, ride your vows to benefit others; though you need not use it yourself, you should test it for the sake of later students, so as to teach those of wisdom to come. If they are of sharp faculties, in one seven-day period or in two they will surely attain single-mindedness. Even for one as dull and slow as I, I suppose that in ten or eight years I may perhaps attain non-distraction."
(Letter to Master Dixian)

[Not failing her grandmotherly heart] Not failing the loving heart of an old grandmother. "Grandmotherly heart" (a Chan phrase) means compassionate, kindly urgings like those of an old grandmother. [The Precious King's method of following the breath] That is the passage above beginning "People in the world mostly use precious stones, crystal, diamond, bodhi seeds, or wooden beads as their recitation beads. I, however, use the out-breath and in-breath as my recitation beads..." This is an instruction from the Precious King Treatise on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, written by Master Feixi of the Tang dynasty; hence it is called the Precious King's method of following the breath. [The five contemplations that still the mind] Contemplations that can still the five faults (greed, anger, delusion, karmic hindrances, and distraction) in the mind. 1. The contemplation of impurity, that is, contemplating that all faculties, bodies, and the material world are impure, in order to still greed. 2. The contemplation of compassion, that is, contemplating the pitiable suffering of all sentient beings, in order to still anger. 3. The contemplation of causes and conditions, that is, contemplating that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, causes preceding and results following, each clearly distinct, in order to still delusion. 4. The contemplation of the Buddha, that is, contemplating the Buddha's bodily marks and the majesty of his virtues, in order to still karmic hindrances. 5. The contemplation of counting the breath, that is, contemplating the arising and passing of the in-breath and the out-breath, silently counting each in-and-out breath from one to ten, in order to still distraction. [Mahāsthāmaprāpta's method of gathering in the six sense faculties] The Chapter on Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation of Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta says: "The Buddha asked about perfect penetration. I had no choice among methods: I gathered in all six sense faculties, and pure mindfulness continued without interruption, and so I attained samādhi. This was foremost." (Translation: When the Buddha asked how perfect penetration is attained, I chose no other method, but gathered in all six faculties, causing deluded thoughts not to arise, with only the mindful recollection of the Buddha continuing unbroken, and thereby attained the samādhi of Buddha-recitation. This way of practice is the foremost and most excellent.) [The six sense faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. [Pure mindfulness continues] The recollection of the Buddha is unbroken. [Samādhi] That is, sanmei (samādhi). [Those of wisdom to come] People of outstanding wisdom in later generations. [I suppose that in ten or eight years I may perhaps attain non-distraction] I suppose that in ten or eight years I will also attain single-minded non-distraction. The word "perhaps" here is a modest expression.
On breath-based Buddha-recitation, Master Tanxu gave this instruction:
"There is also a most convenient method, namely breath-based Buddha-recitation. As you breathe in
(inhalation)
, recite 'Namo A-mi'; as you breathe out, recite 'Tuo-fo.' In this way,
as long as a person has a breath, he recites the Buddha's name once

. In the course of time, at every moment, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, never apart from the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" — this alone is true diligence. When a person is approaching death, at the moment when the last breath is about to cease, the karma of a whole lifetime follows that one recitation of the Buddha made with the final breath, and one goes to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and to see Amitābha Buddha."
Master Tanxu also instructed:

"The practitioner sits upright with the body straight and regulates the breath so that it is neither fast nor slow, neither rough nor gasping; each in-breath and out-breath is calm and slow. Then he recites the Buddha's name following the breath — either the four-character or the six-character form will do, but the four-character form is better. Divide the Buddha's name into two beats: for instance, recite 'A-mi' on the out-breath and 'Tuo-fo' on the in-breath
But one must use abdominal breathing, keep the attention on the lower abdomen, and let it be natural.

This method can be used at rest, in sleep, and whether sitting or standing. If one practices long and becomes thoroughly skilled, so that right mindfulness is not lost, then when the breath ceases one is immediately born in the West,
and this is a supreme method of Buddha-recitation by holding the name
, and those who aspire to the West should take note of it."
The Forty-Eight Methods of Buddha-Recitation by Holding the Name
says:

"Or, when the breath is calm and the mind at peace, first visualize your own body within a circle of light, silently observe the tip of the nose, and attend to the in-breath and out-breath. With each breath
(the out-breath and the in-breath each count as one breath)
silently recite the name of Amitābha Buddha once, skillfully regulating the breath, neither slow nor hurried,
so that mind and breath rely on each other
and follow the breath's going out and coming in.
This may be practiced in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; do not let it be interrupted, but always maintain it quietly.

When the mind has been gathered in for a long time, breath and thought are both forgotten, and this body and mind become equal to empty space. Maintain it until thoroughly skilled, and the eye of the mind opens; samādhi suddenly appears before you — this is the Pure Land of Mind-Only."

The minds of sentient beings are scattered, like wild horses or cunning monkeys, galloping and leaping about without pause for a moment. If one comes to breath-based Buddha-recitation in such a state, with deluded thoughts springing up everywhere, one will find it hard to begin, or hard to keep going, and may even make the body uncomfortable. Therefore, before practicing breath-based Buddha-recitation, it is best first to cultivate the preliminary practices and lay a foundation. The firmer the foundation, the smoother and more effective one's later practice will be.
There are many methods for laying a foundation; for example,
Awareness-Based Buddha-Recitation

introduces a great many of them. The method used in this article is to be aware of the rising and falling (the ascent and descent) of the abdomen, so as to cultivate focused, continuous, and lasting awareness, and thus lay a solid foundation for breath-based Buddha-recitation.

There are chiefly two ways of breathing: chest breathing and abdominal breathing. Chest breathing depends mainly on the movement of the ribs and breastbone; on inhalation the chest expands front to back and side to side. Because the air enters the lungs directly, the chest cavity enlarges and the abdomen stays flat. The breathing used in this article is the natural (forward) form of abdominal breathing, that is, on inhalation the abdominal muscles expand (the abdomen rises) and on exhalation they contract (the abdomen falls),
breathing in and out through the nose
. Compared with chest breathing, this way of breathing brings many benefits to bodily health. (For details, see
Abdominal Breathing

When you inhale, the abdomen gradually rises; at that time simply be aware, with focused attention, of the process of the abdomen rising, and note "up" in the mind. When you exhale, the abdomen gradually falls; at that time simply be aware, with focused attention, of the process of the abdomen falling, and note "down" in the mind. The key point is this: keep continuous awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen. When you first begin to practice, you may place a hand on the abdomen to feel its rising and falling.

So long as you are aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, there will be no deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, that means awareness has been lost, and you must at once draw your attention back and be aware, with focused attention, of the rising and falling of the abdomen. Lost, draw it back; lost, draw it back; ....... If you spend a whole hour in this tug-of-war, that hour has not been wasted. As you practice without cease, you will find that the number of times awareness is lost grows fewer and fewer, and the interval between losing it and drawing it back grows shorter and shorter — that is progress.

When you are fairly sure of your awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen, go a step further and become aware of the sensations within the process of rising and falling (and do not pay attention to the outer shape of the abdomen).

While being aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, if deluded thinking is ablaze and hard to draw back, then do not force yourself to draw it back; instead, observe the deluded thinking with focused attention, watching what it wants to think about, and label it by category: "distracted," "random thinking," or "planning," and so on. When the deluded thinking has weakened, return to being aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen.

In practice there are only these two things: being aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen and observing deluded thinking — and being aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen is primary, the two being applied in flexible alternation.
Outside your dedicated practice time, practice whenever you can seize a spare moment, and try to keep awareness of each movement in your daily activities (see the chapter "Awareness of Movement" in
Awareness Chan

). In short, seize every opportunity to practice awareness and cultivate the power of awareness — this is the basic skill for breath-based Buddha-recitation. Never slight a chance to practice for even two or three minutes!

At the beginning, practice mainly while sitting or lying down. Then gradually extend the practice to walking and standing (while doing walking meditation, or even while walking about in daily life, you may take four steps to one inhalation and four steps to one exhalation). In this way, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, you are always working at the practice; your skill will advance quickly and will adapt easily to circumstances.
When your awareness of the rising and falling of the abdomen is clear and single-pointed, you may enter the stage of Buddha-recitation.
Question: Is noting the same as silently reciting in the mind?

Answer: No. If you silently recite "up" and "down" along with the rising and falling of the abdomen, then once you are familiar with the recitation the following will happen: you have in fact forgotten to be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, yet the mind is still mechanically repeating "up" and "down." Noting, however, is this: when you are aware that the abdomen is rising, you tell yourself that this is "up"; when you are aware that the abdomen is falling, you tell yourself that this is "down." Without awareness, there is no noting.
Thought after thought in unbroken succession, with the end of life as the term; in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, by day and by night, never neglect it.
[Unbroken succession of thoughts] The thoughts of Buddha-recitation connect one to the next, uninterrupted by deluded thoughts.

The method of breath-based Buddha-recitation is this: abdominal breathing in and out through the nose, with the abdomen rising (bulging outward) on inhalation and falling (drawing inward) on exhalation. When you first begin to practice, you may place a hand on the abdomen and feel its rising and falling. As the abdomen rises (inhalation), silently recite "A-mi" in the mind; as the abdomen falls (exhalation), silently recite "Tuo-fo" in the mind. In the initial stage,
while reciting the Buddha's name you must be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen

, and use this as a walking stick. When your skill matures, you no longer pay attention to the rising and falling of the abdomen, but simply recite along with the breath, and there are no deluded thoughts either. If deluded thoughts arise in endless confusion, you must at once pick up the walking stick again: while reciting the Buddha's name, be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen, and the deluded thoughts will be stilled.

Because nine meridians pass through the abdomen, when you practice breath-based Buddha-recitation you are massaging these nine meridians, ensuring harmony of yin and yang in the five viscera and six bowels; at the same time you deepen the breath and increase the lungs' ventilation (the supply of oxygen and the expulsion of carbon dioxide), and so you dispel illness and prolong life. For details, see
The 312 Meridian Health Method (video)

In Buddha-recitation, the thing most to be avoided is drifting with no anchor — reciting on and on while carried off by deluded thoughts, no longer knowing what one is saying. So in the beginning stage, while practicing breath-based recitation, one should also add the method of counting to ten to help still deluded thoughts: count once with each breath, from one to ten (

; bend the little finger at the count of 5 and extend it at the count of 6), then count from one to ten again, over and over without end. When counting, use the bending and extending of the fingers of one hand: with the left hand (the right hand will also do), bend one finger with each breath; when all five fingers are bent, extend one finger with each breath; when all five are extended, that is ten breaths.
To count with the bending and extending of the fingers,
this point is very important

, and you will come to understand its secret in time. When your skill runs deep, you no longer count, and at that time there are no deluded thoughts either. But when in ordinary times you no longer need the walking stick of counting on your fingers, do not forget it. Whenever your mind is vexed and confused, remember (most people do not remember) to pick up this walking stick at once, to help you through the difficult passage. The more vexed and confused you are, the more you should recite the Buddha's name; for thus you can promptly dissolve the entanglements and misfortunes of karmic hindrances, and can also swiftly raise your skill — two gains in one. So the crest of the wind and the tip of the wave is precisely the good opportunity: meet the difficulty head-on and turn vexation and confusion into a favorable condition for progress.

The method of counting to ten has another benefit: each time you reach ten, check how these ten breaths of recitation went. Discover problems promptly and solve them promptly. Then, with mental preparation, rouse your spirits and recite the next ten breaths well. In this way, with immediate feedback and immediate handling, it seems to take time and effort at first, but once you are familiar with it you will do it with ease, and your recitation will grow ever purer. Persevering in this way, you can attain single-minded non-distraction with full confidence.

To make the practice of breath-based Buddha-recitation more fine and subtle, you may also breathe abdominally, slowly, keeping clear account of every breath: within this breath, are there deluded thoughts or not?

When the method of counting to ten has become familiar, you may go further and practice the method of counting to fifty: count once every five breaths, from one to ten (1, 2, 3, ......, 9, 10; bend the little finger at the count of 5 and extend it at the count of 6), then count from one to ten again, over and over without end. When counting, use the bending and extending of the fingers of one hand: with the left hand (the right hand will also do), bend one finger with each breath; when all five fingers are bent, extend one finger with each breath; when all five are extended, that is fifty breaths. Each time you reach ten, check how these fifty breaths of recitation went. Discover problems promptly and solve them promptly. Then, with mental preparation, rouse your spirits and recite the next fifty breaths well. In this way, with immediate feedback and immediate handling, it seems to take time and effort at first, but once you are familiar with it you will do it with ease, and your recitation will grow ever purer. Persevering in this way, you can attain single-minded non-distraction with full confidence.

In practicing the method of counting to fifty, if you continue by bending and extending the fingers of the other hand, you can count one hundred recitations of the Buddha's name. You may also count twice over with one hand, and that too is one hundred recitations.

When you first begin to practice breath-based Buddha-recitation, practice mainly while sitting or lying down. Then gradually extend the practice to walking and standing (while doing walking meditation, or even while walking about in daily life, recite the four-character Buddha's name, one character to a step, four steps to one inhalation and four steps to one exhalation). In this way, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, you are always working at the practice; your skill will advance quickly and will adapt easily to circumstances.

In Buddha-recitation, drifting with no anchor is most to be avoided. During the practice stage of breath-based Buddha-recitation (including breath-based recitation while walking), you must count with the bending and extending of the fingers. In this way the practice proceeds under your control, and every ten breaths or fifty breaths you check: how did the recitation go? What was good about it, what was poor? Keep clear account. Then, on the basis of the feedback, make targeted improvements, working ever more finely and subtly, until you reach single-minded non-distraction.
Seize every spare moment and weave the practice into daily life.

Every night before sleeping, make a brief review: How did my Buddha-recitation go today? What was good, what was poor? How can I improve? How shall I recite tomorrow? Settle the mind on the Way and fall asleep within breath-based Buddha-recitation.
All that has marks is false and delusive
(wisdom)
; not grasping at marks
, one abides unmoved in suchness
(concentration)
Let no thought slip past; let every thought be seen through.
When one is skilled in breath-based Buddha-recitation, one should
go out among conditions
to refine the mind,
consciously
doing
the work of "seeing through and letting go,"
training in every situation the power of concentration and wisdom that does not give rise to mind toward conditions.
To give rise to mind by clinging to conditions is to fall into birth and death; not to give rise to mind toward conditions, and birth and death is ended.
You will find this a most interesting and most wonderful thing —
"not grasping at marks, one abides unmoved in suchness."
With this
one dissolves afflictions and habitual tendencies
and karmic hindrances
, and gradually accomplishes this:
within, not turned by thoughts; without, not dragged by conditions.
This one point is of the utmost importance! Of the utmost importance!
[Not giving rise to mind toward conditions, and birth and death is ended]
The Diamond Sutra says:

"All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, scent, taste, touch, or mental objects; they should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all."
(For annotations, see
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra

Afflictions are many thousands and millions, but summed up they are the three poisons: greed, anger, and delusion. When one's practice of Buddha-recitation gains power, one should use the Buddha's name to subdue afflictions,
purify the mind-ground, and store up provisions for rebirth
. The ancient virtuous ones said:

"When a practitioner's pure karma has matured and his mind-ground is pure, he is in accord with the Buddha; only then, at the end of life, does he see Amitābha Buddha appear before him and lead him to rebirth in the West."

The Buddha's moon is in the sky, its light shining upon millions of minds as upon water. If the mind is impure, like water churned and muddied, then though the moon is in the sky, its reflection does not appear. Hence for one whose thoughts are in confusion at the end of life, though the Buddha sends forth light to receive him, he is like a blind man who cannot see.

[The three poisons] A poison is what harms. Greed, anger, and delusion harm the supramundane wholesome mind, and so are called poisons. 1. The poison of greed: the mind that draws things in and takes them is called greed. When, with a deluded mind, one meets any pleasant object and delights in drawing it in and taking it, this is called the poison of greed. 2. The poison of anger: the mind of resentment and rage is called anger. When, with a deluded mind, one meets any disagreeable object and feels displeasure and loathing, this is called the poison of anger. 3. The poison of delusion: the mind of confusion is called delusion. When one is utterly unclear about the principles and phenomena of all things, takes them up perversely and falsely, and gives rise to wrong actions, this is called the poison of delusion.

Of the three poisons — greed, anger, and delusion — greed is the root, and both anger and delusion arise from greed. Because one cannot obtain the object of craving, or loses what one craves, anger and hatred arise; and because of craving, one goes against principle,
taking things up perversely and falsely,
and so delusion arises. Therefore, to extinguish afflictions, one must work at cutting off craving. The Buddha said:
"Freedom from desire and stillness — this is supreme."
(The Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters Spoken by the Buddha)

Ordinary people cannot be without thought. If they are not mindful of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, they will surely be mindful of greed, anger, and delusion. Being mindful of greed, anger, and delusion, evil karma such as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct arises in swarms, and the wheel of birth and death has no rest. The Buddha, therefore, following the situation and leading it along, seized on the habit of living beings that they cannot be without thought, and skillfully and expediently used a single thought of the Buddha to substitute for false thoughts, causing living beings to turn false thoughts into thoughts of the Buddha and to exchange the defiled mind for a pure mind, and thereby easily to be reborn in the Pure Land and escape from birth and death. Great Master Chewu says:

"The essential of purifying the mind is nothing other than Buddha-recitation. One thought in accord is one thought of Buddha; thought after thought in accord is thought after thought of Buddha. A clear pearl
(a precious pearl that clarifies turbid water)
cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot but become clear; the Buddha-name cast into a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot but become Buddha."

(From the Collected Works of Great Master Chewu.) Therefore, Buddha-recitation is precisely the most intimate and simplest transformation made at the very place closest to a living being's birth and death. And the key to this transformation is:
awareness.
Be aware thought after thought: the moment a false thought arises, immediately use the Buddha-name to turn it away.
One must genuinely and truly carry out this 'awareness
turn it away' practice, letting no single thought slip by, and seeing through each and every thought.
With long practice and deep merit, one naturally fuses into a single whole, subdues the afflictions, and accomplishes the pure karma. The key to purifying the mind is:
use the Buddha-name to turn away false thoughts.
[Awareness thought after thought] In reciting the Buddha-name, be aware of the present thought. See in detail
Aware Buddha-Recitation

the chapter 'Aware of the Present Thought.' [Not letting a single thought slip by] Every false thought, do not let it slide past unbeknownst to you. [Seeing through each thought] Every false thought, do not be enveloped by it, do not listen and follow its play, do not take it as a real matter, and above all do not be kidnapped by it.
To put an end to birth and death, one must know the root of birth and death, and how to uproot it. The patriarchs instruct:

The root of birth and death is precisely the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion; and to uproot the root of birth and death is precisely to spare no effort in the single transformation of a thought in this mind!

One must, amid the realms that appear in daily use, at the times when wife and children gather together, in the dealings among relatives and friends, at the places where right and profit, adverse and favorable, press upon one another, and before joy, anger, greed, and delusion have yet arisen, fix one's gaze and look intently beforehand, and truly, clearly see what is the root of birth and death, and immediately with all one's strength uproot it.
Question: May I practice breath Buddha-recitation while walking?

Answer: Yes. The method is: while walking, silently recite 'Amitabha Buddha,' one character for each step; four steps for an in-breath, four steps for an out-breath. This method, though excellent, is like riding a bicycle: there is a process of learning it, but once mastered, its benefit is inexhaustible. The breathing remains abdominal breathing: on the in-breath the abdomen protrudes, and on the out-breath the abdomen sinks in.
Question: I cannot sustain breath Buddha-recitation for long; after a while I feel tightness in the chest and shortness of breath, very uncomfortable. What should I do?

Answer: The key point of breath Buddha-recitation is to follow the breath. That is, follow the natural breathing and recite the Buddha-name, without controlling or changing the breath. The breathing during breath Buddha-recitation should be the same as your ordinary breathing when not reciting. What you need to do now is carefully come to understand how to follow the breath and recite, working on the word 'follow,' without controlling or changing the breath. First practice in a still state; when your skill in stillness is mature, then gradually practice it in movement.

Question: After practicing breath Buddha-recitation a long time, sometimes I feel the breath is not smooth. Later I used bulging the abdomen and tucking the abdomen to assist abdominal breathing: bulge the abdomen on the in-breath, tuck the abdomen on the out-breath. In this way I solved the problem of the unsmooth breath. May I practice breath Buddha-recitation in this way?
Answer: Yes, entirely.

Question: I have a weak digestive system, and found online that massaging the Sifeng acupoints, pinching the points with the tip of the thumb, can help. So while practicing breath Buddha-recitation, I also pinch the Sifeng acupoints. The method is: on the in-breath recite 'Ami' (Amita), and on the out-breath recite 'Tuofo' (-buddha), and pinch the acupoint on the out-breath; pinch one acupoint on each out-breath, pinching each acupoint five times, silently counting in the mind, and so on in rotation. (You may also do it with a single hand, using the thumb to pinch the Sifeng acupoints of the same hand.) After a period of time, the old ailment of my digestive system was cured, and I found that reciting the Buddha-name in this way not only gathers the mind and resists distraction, but is also easy to sustain. My question is: may I recite the Buddha-name in this way?

Answer: Your method is similar to pinching the prayer beads while reciting the Buddha-name; both are crutches, and help to gather the mind. The advantage of pinching acupoints is that it is not restricted by circumstances: in meetings, in conversation, while sleeping, and so on, it can all be done. If you feel it gathers the mind, resists distraction, and is easy to sustain (a Buddha-recitation method is good if it satisfies these three conditions), then of course you may recite the Buddha-name in this way. At the same time, you should put more effort into deep faith and resolute vows.

In response to fellow practitioners' request, the questioner answered: Let me describe the specific method I now use, of 'breath Buddha-recitation while also pinching the Sifeng acupoints,' for everyone's reference. The main points are three: first, the breathing remains abdominal breathing: on the in-breath the abdomen protrudes, and on the out-breath the abdomen sinks in. On the in-breath recite 'Ami,' and on the out-breath recite 'Tuofo.' Second, pinch the acupoints on the out-breath. With both hands, use each thumb to pinch the Sifeng acupoints of that same hand, pinching one acupoint on each out-breath and pinching each acupoint once, in order: index finger, middle finger, ring finger, little finger; little finger, ring finger, middle finger, index finger; index finger, middle finger, ring finger, little finger; and so on in this cycle. Third, at the same time, be focused and continuously aware of the Buddha-name, clearly knowing the thought-mark of the Buddha-name (how each character is produced), and whether there is only the thought of reciting the Buddha. I use this method whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; only when walking is it one character per step, four steps for an in-breath, four steps for an out-breath, while the method of pinching the acupoints and being aware of the Buddha-name remains unchanged.

Question: I tried the above acupoint-pinching method for a while and found it gathers the mind well. But since my digestive system has no ailment, doing this seems cumbersome. Is there a simpler method?

Answer: You may replace pinching the acupoints with the opening and closing of the palms, single hand or both hands. On the in-breath, the palm opens flat and the abdomen protrudes, reciting 'Ami'; on the out-breath, the palm closes and the abdomen sinks in, reciting 'Tuofo.' Once skilled, the opening and closing of the palms may be done slightly, so slightly that others will not notice; in short, what is comfortable, convenient, and sustainable is best. At the same time, be focused and continuously aware of the Buddha-name, clearly knowing the thought-mark of the Buddha-name (how each character is produced), and whether there is only the thought of reciting the Buddha.

Even so, whether pinching acupoints or opening and closing the palms, after all both are auxiliary movements. Once you have fully mastered breath Buddha-recitation, when you feel it is no longer necessary, you may leave these crutches behind.
Question: May I cultivate the Buddha-recitation samadhi through breath Buddha-recitation?
Answer: Yes. The Buddha-recitation samadhi aims at realizing the mind and seeing the nature (see in detail
Record of Groping at the Features of the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi

). For this, you should follow the breath Buddha-recitation method described above and attain one mind undisturbed. Then, on this foundation, cultivate the Buddha-recitation samadhi, in order to realize and enter the state of seeing the nature. The method is: while practicing breath Buddha-recitation, from the mysterious gate, turn the inner light down upon the lower dantian. If a false thought arises, it shows the inner light is scattered, not focused, not continuous. You should immediately bestir yourself and refocus the inner light, and the false thought will subside of itself. Practicing thus for a long time, when effort reaches its utmost and the practice becomes a pure, single whole, suddenly the thought of recitation falls away, and one realizes and enters the state of no-thought and yet no-thoughtlessness.
[The mysterious gate] Also called the upper dantian, located at the third eye (the heavenly eye).

[The lower dantian] This is the Guanyuan point of the Conception Vessel, located three cun below the navel (about four fingers' width), and is the place where the essence is stored. The lower dantian is the principal place for training, gathering, and storing the true qi. A person's primordial qi originates in the kidneys and is stored in the dantian, and by way of the three burners circulates throughout the body, driving the functional activity of the five organs and six viscera. The strength or weakness of the body, indeed life and death, all depend on the flourishing or decline of the dantian's primordial qi; therefore the care of the dantian's primordial qi is extremely important. When the dantian's primordial qi is full and vigorous, it can mobilize the body's potential and cause the true qi to circulate through the whole body. Fixing the attention on the dantian can regulate yin and yang, connect the heart and kidneys, make the true qi full, free the eight vessels, restore the prenatal physiological functions, and promote the body's health and longevity.

[Practicing thus for a long time] This is prajna perfuming ignorance; the moment ignorance is broken, the dharmakaya suddenly manifests. [When effort reaches its utmost and the practice becomes pure] The effort is used to the utmost, and the practice becomes a single, pure whole. [Suddenly] A description of openness and penetration; for example, 'suddenly open and bright,' 'suddenly penetrating and connected,' 'suddenly awakened.' 'Suddenly' also indicates the appearance of awakening; for example, the Family Instructions of Mr. Yan says: 'The years of obstruction and stagnation, suddenly dissolve like mist (the mist disperses).' Su Xun, in his First Letter to Inner-Han Ouyang, says: 'And after a long time, the more one reads it the finer it becomes, and in one's chest it is suddenly open and bright.' [The thought and the recitation fall away together] Both subject and object vanish, that is, the mind that recites and the Buddha that is recited fall away at the same time.
In cultivating the Buddha-recitation samadhi there are several points to note: first, it is best to have from the start some understanding of the true reality of all dharmas (see in detail
The True Reality of All Dharmas
article
) and of the original nature (see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha
article

); second, if any realms arise in the practice, one must neither receive nor cling to them, and only then can one advance; third, off the cushion one must refine the mind amid circumstances, not being turned by them, in order to truly realize the original nature.
Question: While investigating the Buddha-recitation, my false thoughts have grown far fewer, but when drowsiness overwhelms me, I am at a loss. How should I counteract the drowsiness?

Answer: You may counteract the drowsiness in this way. Bestir your spirit, and from time to time raise your head and look upward, and do deep abdominal breathing: inhale deeply through the nose (abdomen protruding), hold the breath for
second, then exhale slowly (abdomen sinking in), hold the breath for
second, and keep one cycle of inhalation and exhalation to about

seconds. At the same time, recite the Buddha-name and be clearly aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen. In this way the drowsiness will gradually disperse. Once the drowsiness has gone, return to your original way of reciting the Buddha-name.
